project.title: A statistical report on real Nigerian data

blocks.text: Write a two-page statistical report on a public Nigerian dataset. You can use the offline extract below or choose another public Nigerian series with at least ten comparable observations and published metadata. Use a spreadsheet, paper or the in-app Python tool. Keep any original extracts separate from your working table.

## Source and question Use a question the observations can answer. For the offline extract, ask “How did Nigeria's estimated infant mortality rate vary from 2014 through 2023, and how sensitive is the endpoint comparison to the start year?” Each row is one national calendar-year estimate, not one child or an estimate for one clinic. The unit is per 1,000 live births.

Source: World Development Indicators, Nigeria, indicator SP.DYN.IMRT.IN, from the UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation. Snapshot retrieved 6 November 2026, API metadata last updated 8 October 2026. Retrieve the same range by searching the indicator code and selecting Nigeria and 2014–2023, or use this dated extract if the online series has since changed.
Source page: https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SP.DYN.IMRT.IN?locations=NG
## What to submit

items: State the question, unit of observation, population or geography, reference period and the source version. Include the original table or a dated extract that can be reproduced.
Audit the data. Check duplicate dates, missing values, units and comparability. Record any changes or exclusions with reasons. For the provided extract, retain all ten values.

Calculate a measure of centre and a measure of spread with units. For the provided series, compute the median and IQR under the median-of-halves rule. Explain what variability across years measures, and why it does not give the uncertainty of each annual estimate.

Draw a chart that fits the question. For annual estimates, put years in order and label the rate scale. Use a caption that someone can read without the surrounding prose. Report absolute and relative endpoint changes with their distinct units.
Repeat one reasonable choice as a sensitivity check. For the provided series, compare 2014–2023 with 2018–2023. Show whether the size or direction of the endpoint change differs.

Conclude with one supported finding, one limit and one follow-up question. Do not use an aggregate time series to infer an individual outcome or a cause. Where uncertainty bounds are unavailable in the extract, say you used point estimates.

rubric: I named the exact source, release or snapshot, population, period and measurement units.
My working table preserves original observations and records any exclusions or corrections.
Another reader can reproduce my centre, spread and endpoint comparisons from my calculations.
My chart has a meaningful scale, labelled axes and a caption with the source and scope.
I reported a sensitivity check and distinguished variation over time from uncertainty about individual estimates.
My conclusion stays within the evidence and proposes a useful follow-up.

lessons.title: What statistics is, and the kinds of data
lessons.source: OpenStax · Introductory Statistics 2e · Chapter 1
lessons.goal: Say what statistics is, tell descriptive from inferential statistics, and classify any variable as categorical or numerical, discrete or continuous, and by its level of measurement.
lessons.why: This is where a statistics degree begins, and it's usually the first thing tested. The kind of data you have decides every later choice: which chart to draw, which average to use, and which test to run. Using the wrong method for the data type gives answers that look fine and mean nothing. If you get this right now, a lot of later statistics becomes a simple matter of following the type.

blocks.text: **Statistics** is the science of collecting, organising, summarising and interpreting data, and of making decisions when you can't be certain. **Data** are recorded facts, such as ages, test scores or the state each student comes from. One recorded fact is a **data value**, or **observation**.

Why does it exist? Because things vary. Students in one class get different scores, and prices differ from market to market. If everything were the same, one measurement would tell you everything. Statistics is how you see the pattern through that variation.
The subject has two main branches.

head: Branch
What it does
Example
rows: The average score in this class was 58
Uses a sample to draw conclusions about a larger group, with stated uncertainty
Based on 200 students, about 40% of all students at the school work part-time

blocks.text: STA 111 focuses on the first. Inference comes later, and needs the probability you'll build along the way.

blocks.question: "In last week's quiz, the highest mark was 18 out of 20." Is that descriptive or inferential?
blocks.answer: Descriptive. It only summarises the marks that exist, and makes no claim about anyone else.

blocks.text: A **variable** is a characteristic that can differ from one item to the next. Each item studied is a **unit** or **case**. Data usually sit in a table, with one row per case and one column per variable.
Here the cases are students, and the variables are level, state, courses and height. These are invented values, for illustration.
The first question to ask of any variable is whether its values are categories or real quantities.

Treating anything written in digits as numerical. A matric number, phone number or postcode is digits used as a label. The average of your class's phone numbers means nothing. The test is whether adding or averaging the values would mean anything.
Numerical variables split again.

head: Type
Values
Test
Examples
rows: Separate values, with gaps between them, usually from counting
Number of siblings, courses, or failed logins
Any value in a range, usually from measuring

blocks.text: You can't have 2.5 siblings, but a height can be 172.53 cm if your ruler is good enough. Measurements get rounded in practice, but the variable is still continuous. Money is an awkward case, since it comes in smallest units, yet it's often treated as continuous when the amounts are large.

blocks.question: Is the number of files in a folder discrete or continuous? And the size of one file in megabytes?
blocks.answer: The number of files is discrete, since you count them. File size is usually treated as continuous, because it's measured over a wide range, although at the deepest level it's a count of bytes.

blocks.text: Variables are also classified by what comparisons they support. Many Nigerian statistics courses teach this, so learn the four levels in order. Each level adds a property to the one before.

head: Level
You can
Example
Average that fits
rows: Also put them in order, but gaps aren't equal
Grade A to F, 100 to 400 level, "agree" to "disagree"
Also measure equal gaps, but zero isn't "none"
Also compare by ratio, as zero means none

blocks.text: The tell for interval versus ratio is zero. 0 degrees Celsius doesn't mean no temperature, so 20 degrees isn't twice as hot as 10 degrees. But N0 really means no money, so N200 is truly twice N100.
The tell for ordinal is uneven gaps. The gap between "agree" and "strongly agree" isn't a measured quantity. An A isn't exactly as far from a B as a B is from a C.
Worked example: classify everything
Textbooks and lecturers can differ on borderline cases, such as whether star ratings may be treated as numbers. In an exam, follow your course material and lecturer.

**Primary data** are collected by you for your purpose, through surveys, experiments or observation. **Secondary data** were collected by somebody else, such as the National Bureau of Statistics, and you reuse them. Secondary data are cheaper, but you need to check how they were collected and what they actually measure.
Data can also be **cross-sectional**, a snapshot at one time, or **time series**, the same thing tracked over time, such as monthly inflation.

warmup.question: What does a row in a simple record often stand for?
warmup.answer: One thing observed, such as one journey. The question determines which thing.

warmup.question: If two buses each have a route number, does adding the route numbers measure anything?
warmup.answer: No. They identify routes rather than measuring a quantity.

blocks.text: Use your own real information. Make a small data table on paper or in a spreadsheet.

items: Choose something you can record at least 8 times, such as your study sessions, your courses, or your spending. Each row is one case.

Record at least five variables per case. Try to include at least one categorical and one numerical variable. Example: for a study session, record the course, the date, the minutes, how focused you felt from 1 to 5, and how many questions you tried.
Classify every variable as categorical or numerical, then discrete or continuous if it's numerical, then its level.
For each, say whether averaging makes sense, and why.
Keep this table. You'll use it to make charts and averages in the next lessons.

blocks.text: Describe your variables and their classifications. Leave out private details.

rubric: I recorded real data of my own, with at least five variables.
I classified every variable, and gave a reason for at least the hard ones.
I kept my table for the next lessons.

exercises.question: Classify "marital status".
exercises.answer: Categorical and nominal. Its values are labels with no natural order.

exercises.question: Classify "position in class: 1st, 2nd, 3rd".
exercises.answer: Ordinal. There's an order, but the gap between 1st and 2nd isn't necessarily equal to that between 2nd and 3rd.

exercises.question: Is "the number of fraud cases per month" discrete or continuous? What's its level?
exercises.answer: Discrete, because it's a count. Ratio, because zero means none, and 20 cases is twice 10.

exercises.question: "Temperature was 15 degrees yesterday and 30 degrees today, so today is twice as hot." What's wrong?
exercises.answer: Celsius is interval, since zero isn't no temperature. You can say it's 15 degrees warmer, but not twice as hot.

summary: Descriptive statistics summarises what you have. Inferential statistics draws conclusions about more.
A variable is a characteristic that differs. Each row is a case.
Categorical values are labels. Numerical values are amounts. Digits can still be labels.
Discrete values are counted, and continuous values are measured.
Nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio each add a property. Only ratio has a true zero.

lessons.title: Turn counts into a proportion
lessons.source: OpenStax · Prealgebra 2e · Understand Percent
lessons.goal: Define what you are counting, calculate fractions, proportions and percentages correctly, and spot when a percentage on its own is misleading.
lessons.why: Statistics is built on this one idea: a number only means something next to what it was counted out of. It is also your best defence against misleading claims, which you will meet constantly in the news, in adverts, and later in fraud work. "90% of customers agreed" sounds strong until you learn that ten people were asked. This lesson also underpins your whole statistics degree.

blocks.text: Before you count, say exactly what one item is and which items qualify. "How many of my files are PDFs?" sounds clear, but raises questions. Do files inside subfolders count? Do shortcuts count? A count is only useful if someone else could follow your rule and get the same number. Statisticians call each counted item a **unit** or **observation**, and the group of all eligible items the **reference group** or the **base**.
Worked example: writing a counting rule
Vague: "the number of my courses that are hard".
Clear: "the number of courses I am registered for this semester in which I scored below 50 in my last test".
The clear version names the group, the time and the test for qualifying. If you can't write a rule like that, you aren't ready to count.

A **proportion** is a part divided by its whole. The **numerator** on top is the number that qualify. The **denominator** on the bottom is the size of the whole reference group, including those that qualify.

blocks.code:
proportion = number that qualify / number in the whole group
percentage = proportion x 100

blocks.text: Worked example
A folder has 40 files, of which 10 are PDFs.
**Percent** just means "per hundred". To convert a fraction, divide and multiply by 100. To go from a percentage back to a decimal, divide by 100, so 7% is 0.07, not 0.7.
Using the wrong denominator. The denominator is the whole group, not "the others". With 10 PDFs and 30 other files, the proportion of PDFs is 10/40, not 10/30.

blocks.question: 18 of the 60 students in a class are absent. What percentage is absent?

blocks.text: Three calculations cover nearly everything you will meet.

head: You want
Do this
Example
rows: What percentage A is of B

blocks.text: Percentage change
Percentage change compares a change with the **starting** value.

Bread goes from N800 to N1,000. The change is 200, and 200 / 800 is 25%, so it rose 25%. Now suppose it falls back from N1,000 to N800. The change is the same N200, but 200 / 1000 is only 20%. The base is different, so the percentage is different. A rise of 25% is undone by a fall of 20%, not 25%.
Percentage points

If a pass rate goes from 40% to 50%, it rose by **10 percentage points**, but by **25 percent**, since 10 / 40 is 0.25. Both are correct statements about the same change, and the difference is often used to make a change sound bigger or smaller than it is.

blocks.question: An exam fee rises from ₦5,000 to ₦6,000, then the next year falls by 20%. What is it now?
blocks.answer: ₦6,000 is a 20% rise. Falling 20% from ₦6,000 removes ₦1,200, leaving ₦4,800. It doesn't return to ₦5,000, since each percentage applies to a different base.

blocks.text: A percentage hides the size of its group, so always report both. Compare:

head: Claim
Counts behind it
How much it should convince you

blocks.text: With a small group, one case swings the result wildly. Moving one person in a group of 5 shifts the percentage by 20 points, whereas in a group of 1,000 it moves 0.1 points. So a change from 2 of 5 to 3 of 5 is a 20-point jump, caused by one person.
Before you trust a percentage, yours or someone else's, ask these.

items: **Of what?** What is the denominator? "60% of graduates" means something different from "60% of those who responded".
**How many?** What are the counts behind it?
**Does it make sense?** A part of a group can't be above 100%. If nothing qualifies, it's 0%.
**Is it defined?** If the group is empty, you would divide by zero. There is no answer, not even zero. Say the group was empty.

blocks.text: Percentages can go above 100% when they compare with a starting value rather than a part of a whole. A price that goes from N100 to N300 has risen by 200%, and that's a correct statement.

warmup.question: What makes a numeric code a category rather than a measurement?
warmup.answer: Its meaning is a label. Arithmetic on it has no useful interpretation.

warmup.question: What fraction is 25%?

blocks.text: Use real counts from your own life. Don't use anyone else's private information.

items: Choose a real group you can count now, such as the files in one study folder, your courses this semester, or the days this month you studied.
Write a counting rule that someone else could follow. Say what one item is, which items are in the group and which qualify.
Count the qualifying items and the whole group.

Write the two counts, the simplified fraction, the proportion and the percentage. Do the arithmetic by hand, then check it in the Python box below. In the Python box below, each `print` line shows a result when you press **Run Python**. You don't need to know Python yet. Just change the numbers.
Change one item, for example add a file. Recalculate and write down how much one item moved the percentage.

blocks.text: If your group is empty, write that the proportion is undefined and why.

rubric: My counting rule is specific enough for another person to follow.
I reported both counts next to the percentage.
I worked out how much one item moves the percentage.
practice.starter:
# Put your own counts here: qualifying items, then the whole group
print(10 / 40)
print(10 / 40 * 100)

exercises.question: A bank says 3 in every 200 transfers it checked were fraudulent. Express this as a percentage.
exercises.answer: 3 divided by 200 is 0.015, which is 1.5%.

exercises.question: 35% of a class of 80 passed. How many students passed?
A channel's views go from 400 to 500, and then 500 to 400. Calculate each percentage change.
exercises.answer: Up 25% (100 / 400), then down 20% (100 / 500). The base changed.

exercises.question: A survey claims 100% satisfaction. What is the first thing you should ask?
exercises.answer: How many people responded, and how they were chosen. It could be very few, and only people likely to be happy.

summary: Define the group and the rule before you count.
A proportion is the part divided by the whole, and the whole includes the part.
Percent means per hundred, so divide by 100 to get the decimal. 7% is 0.07.
Percentage change divides by the starting value, so up 25% is undone by down 20%.
Report counts alongside percentages. A small group makes percentages jumpy. An empty group has no proportion.

lessons.title: Population and sample
lessons.source: OpenStax · Introductory Statistics 2e · Section 1.1
lessons.goal: Separate a population from a sample, tell a parameter from a statistic, and name the sampling bias in a real study, including why a bigger sample doesn't fix it.
lessons.why: Nearly every question in your statistics degree asks what a sample can tell you about something larger. Getting this wrong produces confident nonsense, which is why it's the first thing a good analyst checks. It is also directly useful: most misleading claims about money, health or scams fail at this exact point, and you will soon build a channel around checking such claims.

blocks.text: Statistics begins when you want to know something about a group too large to look at completely.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: The whole group your question is about
All undergraduates at one university this session
The true average weekly study hours of all of them
A number calculated from the sample
The thing that differs between units

blocks.text: Here's an easy way to remember the pair: **p**arameter goes with **p**opulation, and **s**tatistic goes with **s**ample. You usually can't know a parameter, so you use a statistic to estimate it.
A population is not always people. It is whatever your conclusion covers: all transactions last year, every day of this term, all light bulbs from a factory.
Be specific about who or what, where and when, because each choice changes the answer.
Vague: "Do students study a lot?"
Clear: "What is the average number of hours per week that 100-level students at your university study outside class during this semester?"
Now the population is clear, so you can judge whether any sample really represents it.
Worked example: identify each part
A researcher wants to know the proportion of Port Harcourt small businesses that accept bank transfers. She visits 120 shops along one main road and finds that 90 do.

items: **Population:** all small businesses in Port Harcourt.
**Sample:** the 120 shops she visited.
**Parameter:** the true proportion across all of them, which is unknown.
**Statistic:** 90/120, or 75%.

blocks.question: What's the problem with her sample, given the question she asked?
blocks.answer: Shops on one main road may differ from the rest, as they could be busier, better off, or more connected. So 75% may overstate the proportion for the whole city.

blocks.text: A sample is **biased** when the way it was collected makes some members of the population more likely to be included in a way that distorts the result. These are the common kinds.

head: Type
What goes wrong
Example
rows: You use whoever is easy to reach
Asking only your friends about a lecturer
People choose whether to take part
An online poll, answered mostly by those who feel strongly
Part of the population can't be reached
An online survey of a town where many have no data
Many who are chosen don't reply, and they differ
People with low results ignore a survey on results
You only see those who lasted
Studying only successful businesses to learn what works

blocks.text: Believing a large sample cures bias. It does not. A million self-selected online voters still only represent people who chose to vote in that poll. A larger sample drawn the same biased way can narrow sampling variability while leaving the systematic error.

Survivorship is worth remembering if you plan to earn online. You mostly hear from people whose channels succeeded, and almost never from the many whose channels did not. Conclusions drawn from the winners alone will mislead you.

In a **simple random sample**, every member of the population has the same chance of selection, and every possible group of that size is equally likely. Randomness protects you from your own preferences, and from unmeasured differences that you would never think to check.
To do this you need a **sampling frame**, a list of the population to draw from. Other designs you will meet in Sampling and Experiments are:

items: **Stratified:** split the population into groups, such as levels of study, and sample randomly within each.
**Systematic:** pick a random start, then take every kth item from a list.
**Cluster:** randomly choose whole groups, such as hostels, then study everyone in them.

blocks.text: A computer can draw a random sample. Here is how it looks in Python, which you'll learn soon. A fixed seed makes the draw repeatable, which matters when you need to show your work:

blocks.code:
import random
random.seed(1)
days = list(range(1, 31))
print(random.sample(days, 5))

sections.title: What a sample can and cannot tell you

blocks.text: Different samples give different statistics, even without any bias. This natural variation is called **sampling variability**, and larger samples from the same sound design usually reduce it. So size helps with chance error, while good selection deals with bias. You need both.

blocks.code:
Bias: errors from how the sample was chosen. Size doesn't fix it.
Sampling variability: errors from chance. A larger sample reduces it.

blocks.text: When you report a result, state who was sampled, how they were chosen, how many, and when. Then limit your claim to what that supports. "Among the 30 days I recorded" is honest. "I always study this much" may not be.

warmup.question: Why should a percentage always name its denominator?
warmup.answer: It tells you which group the numerator comes from.

warmup.question: Which unit would you record when comparing waiting time for individual trips?
warmup.answer: One trip, with a defined start and end.

blocks.text: Choose a real question about your own life or your own files that needs no one else's private information. For example: "What's my average sleep on school nights this term?" or "What proportion of my study files have been opened this month?"

items: Write the question, specific in who or what, where and when.
Name your population, your sample, the parameter you want, and the statistic you will calculate.
Name two ways your sample could differ from the population, using the bias types above.

In the Python box below, change 30 to the size of your population and 5 to your sample size, then press **Run Python**. It draws a simple random sample of item numbers. You don't need to know Python yet. Write what you would change to reduce the bias.

rubric: I named the population and sample for a real question of my own.
I named specific bias risks, and why they would push the result.
I described a change that deals with bias, and not only a larger sample.
practice.starter:
import random
# Change 30 to your population size and 5 to your sample size
items = list(range(1, 31))
print(random.sample(items, 5))

exercises.question: A company wants staff views on pay. It emails a survey to all staff, and 12% reply. Name the likely bias.
exercises.answer: Non-response, and self-selection. Those who reply may feel more strongly than those who don't.

exercises.question: A statistic or a parameter? "Of the 500 voters polled, 52% support the plan."
exercises.answer: A statistic, because it was calculated from the sample of 500.

exercises.question: A study of 2 million people finds a result, but everyone in it volunteered through one app. Does the size make it reliable about everybody?
exercises.answer: No. It's still biased toward users of that app who chose to take part. Size reduces chance error, not selection error.

exercises.question: You want to estimate your average daily study time this term. You record only days you feel you worked hard. What happens to your estimate?
exercises.answer: It will be too high. The rule for including days favours larger values.

summary: The population is the whole group you want to know about, and the sample is what you observe.
A parameter describes a population. A statistic describes a sample.
Bias comes from how a sample is chosen. A larger biased sample is still biased.
Random selection gives every member the same chance and protects against unseen differences.
Report who, how, how many and when, then limit your claim to that.

lessons.title: Collecting data honestly
lessons.source: Statistics Canada · Questions to ask about surveys
lessons.goal: Turn a question into a repeatable collection plan. Record missing results and corrections without hiding what happened.
lessons.why: A precise calculation cannot repair an unclear question or a missing part of the record. A collection plan makes it possible to find the problem while there is still time to fix it.

blocks.text: Start with the decision your data should help you make. Suppose you want to know whether morning or afternoon practice sessions are easier to start on time. “Did I have a good week?” will not tell you that. A question you can actually record is “Of the practice sessions I scheduled this week, what proportion began within ten minutes of the planned start, by time of day?” The comparison is about that particular week and those sessions.

The observation unit is one scheduled session, including sessions you did not start. Give each session one row. Record the scheduled time, actual start if it happened, and status. Decide whether exactly ten minutes late counts before you see any results. Here it counts. A scheduled session you deliberately cancelled should stay in the log with the status cancelled. Decide ahead of time whether you will include it in the primary denominator and explain that decision in the result. You can also report cancellations separately. A session that was never scheduled is outside the scope.

A **measurement protocol** tells you how to collect each value. Write both times to the nearest minute using the same clock. Define morning using the scheduled time rather than the actual start so a delayed morning session cannot move itself into the afternoon group. If someone else could read your rules and record the same session the same way, the definition is doing its job.

If you collect other people's answers, ask one neutral thing at a time. “How convenient and affordable was the trip?” asks two different things. Someone can find it convenient but expensive. “How many minutes did your most recent trip take, from leaving your starting point to arriving?” asks for one measure and gives a time reference. Offer a way to say “don't know” if someone cannot remember. Collect only what you need, tell people how you will use it, and let them decline. Anonymous summaries are enough for this course. Names, account numbers and precise home addresses are unnecessary.

Before a full collection, try the plan on a few cases. This small trial is a **pilot**. Ask a participant to explain what the question meant to them. If two people use different starting points, revise the question. Label pilot rows and do not silently merge them with final rows when a definition changed. A repeated measurement can also reveal a measurement problem. If two readings differ, check the tool and write which reading you kept and why.

For an illustration from real data collection, the National Bureau of Statistics publishes a catalogue entry for the Nigeria Labour Force Survey. It describes what the survey measures and links to reports and documentation. That record makes it possible to inspect definitions and data collection decisions rather than guessing from the headline. For a home study log, a short note above your table serves the same purpose.

Use distinct codes for distinct events. Zero delay means a start at the planned time. No start means the event did not happen. An unrecorded start means you do not know the time. These three situations answer different questions. Keep blanks or a clearly documented code for missing values, and record the reason where known. Replacing missing times with zero makes the average delay appear smaller without any evidence.
Worked example: one week's log
These eight scheduled sessions are invented. An arrival ten minutes late still counts as on time.

head: Question
Numerator and denominator
Result
rows: Of sessions with a known start, how many started on time?
5 on time out of 6 known starts
Of all scheduled sessions, how many are confirmed on time?

blocks.text: The second row does not claim the unknown start was late. Both counts use the same record and answer different questions.

Keep an untouched copy of your original observations. If a timestamp was entered as 09:20 instead of 09:02, record the old value, the new value, and the evidence for the correction. If a value merely looks unusual, check it rather than deleting it. At the end, count eligible rows and compare that count with the record you expected. Report the missing rows alongside your summary. A clean-looking table is useful only when someone can reconstruct how it became clean.

warmup.question: A neighbourhood survey is answered only by people who see an online post. What may be missing?
warmup.answer: Residents without access to the post, and residents who see it but do not reply.

warmup.question: What do you need beside a reported proportion?
warmup.answer: The numerator, eligible denominator and the rule used to count each.

blocks.text: Choose one harmless question about your own routine or a set of public records. Define the row, eligibility, unit, threshold and missing codes. Pilot three observations. Revise one unclear rule if needed. Collect at least five observations with the final definition and write a one-sentence summary that states how many values were missing.

rubric: Another person could apply my rules to the same observation.
I preserved missing and cancelled observations and stated how I counted them.
I recorded any change between pilot and final collection.

exercises.question: On Monday the second session started exactly ten minutes late. Which status does it get?
exercises.answer: On time, because the stated rule includes exactly ten minutes.

exercises.question: A learner enters 0 where their timer stopped recording. What should change?
exercises.answer: Use a missing code and record the reason. Keep 0 only for a measured zero.

exercises.question: Why group sessions by scheduled start rather than actual start?
exercises.answer: Grouping by the actual start can move the latest morning sessions into the afternoon and hide a morning delay.

summary: Define the unit and eligibility before collecting.
Pilot neutral questions and consistent measurements.
Keep missing values distinct from zero and preserve the original record.

lessons.title: Where official data comes from
lessons.source: National Bureau of Statistics · Nigeria Labour Force Survey catalogue
lessons.goal: Trace an official number to its table, population and reference period. Tell a census, sample survey and administrative record apart.
lessons.why: Two numbers can both be published by trustworthy organisations and still describe different things. Knowing where they came from tells you what they can answer.

blocks.text: A **census** attempts to observe every eligible unit in a defined population. A population census tries to cover people or households according to its census rules. A census can still miss some units or contain errors. “Everyone was intended to be covered” and “everyone was counted correctly” are different claims. A **sample survey** observes a selected part of the population. Official releases use a documented design and may weight observations so that sampled units contribute different amounts to the estimate. A simple count of rows in the survey file need not match a published national percentage.

An **administrative record** is created while providing a service or carrying out a rule. Birth registrations, examination records and clinic visits are examples. These records can measure activity among people reached by that system. They may miss events outside it. A record of births registered in April is not automatically a count of babies born in April. Registration may occur after a birth, and some births may never appear in the register. Check which date and which people the table counts before drawing a conclusion.

Sources can be combined. A population estimate can start from a census and use estimates of births, deaths and migration to estimate later years. An annual figure in the World Bank's Nigeria population series does not imply an annual head count. Read the indicator's source information and identify the observation as a count or an estimate in your notes.

sections.title: Read the release beside the number

blocks.text: Open the National Bureau of Statistics catalogue entry for the Nigeria Labour Force Survey. Follow its documentation or related materials to the release you want. The catalogue describes an actual survey series. A quarterly labour statistic refers to a particular reference period, even when its report was released much later. In a spreadsheet record the data period separately from the publication date. If you downloaded the file this morning, that is a third date and belongs in your source log.

**Metadata** are the details that make values interpretable. For each column write the measure, population, geography, units, time period, producer and release version. A published rate also needs a denominator. For example, an unemployment rate concerns the labour force as defined by the survey, rather than everyone living in the country. A percentage for the whole country and a percentage for one state also answer different questions. Their labels are part of the data.

The catalogue for the Nigeria Multidimensional Poverty Index links to the 2022 report and survey materials. A multidimensional measure uses specified indicators and rules about deprivation. A share classified by those rules cannot be treated as the share below an income threshold just because both have “poverty” in their name. Read the method section for the actual construction, and quote the report title rather than copying an unattributed screenshot.
Worked example: logging one official number

Look up Nigeria's annual infant mortality indicator in World Development Indicators. Select the 2023 row. The World Bank API snapshot retrieved on 6 November 2026 lists 70.1. Save the number beside its definition rather than as a bare figure.

A household survey estimates 300 births that occurred in April. It would be tempting to divide 240 by 300 and report 80% registration coverage. You cannot do that without knowing that the 240 certificates refer to births from the same eligible group and birth period. The numerator may include children born in March. Use a matched numerator or report the two figures separately.

For a public exercise you can save the public extract locally. Avoid including private microdata in a report. lessons.title: Frequency tables and charts
lessons.source: OpenStax · Introductory Statistics 2e · Section 2.1 and 2.2
lessons.goal: Build a frequency table with relative and cumulative frequencies, group numerical data into classes, choose the right chart for a variable, and spot a chart that misleads.
lessons.why: A column of raw numbers can make patterns hard to spot. A good table or chart lets you see how often different values occur. Practise making both by hand so you can check the result when a tool makes one for you. For example, a fraud analyst can use a chart of transaction amounts to decide which unusual records deserve a closer look.

sections.title: From raw data to a frequency table

blocks.text: A **frequency** is how many times a value occurs. A **frequency distribution** lists each value, or group of values, and its frequency.
Worked example: a categorical variable
20 students (invented data) give their favourite way to pay.
**Relative frequency** is a frequency divided by the total. Always check your totals: frequencies must add up to the number of cases, and relative frequencies to 1, apart from small rounding.
By hand, people often use **tally marks**: a stroke for each value, with every fifth stroke crossing the previous four, so that they can be counted in fives.
If a variable has many different values, listing each is no use. Group them into **classes**, which are intervals.
Worked example: test scores
Scores of 20 students (invented):
**Step 1: choose classes.** The range is 91 - 34 = 57. About 5 to 10 classes usually works. Take a width of 10, starting at 30.
**Step 2: count into classes.** Each value must fall in exactly one class, so classes can't overlap.
**Cumulative frequency** is a running total. It answers questions such as "how many scored under 70?" That's 14, read straight from the table.
Python can count this for you, once you've done it by hand:

Terms you'll see in textbooks. **Class limits** are the stated ends, such as 30 and 39. **Class boundaries** close the gaps between classes, as in 29.5 to 39.5. The **class mark** or midpoint is (30 + 39) / 2 = 34.5, and the **class width** is 10. You'll need these for calculating with grouped data, so learn the form your course uses.

blocks.question: From the table, how many students scored 60 or more?
blocks.answer: 6 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 12. Or use the cumulative column: 20 total minus the 8 below 60 gives 12.

lessons.title: Grouped data
lessons.source: Statistics Canada · Statistics: Power from Data
lessons.goal: Build nonoverlapping classes, tally measurements and explain what grouping hides.
lessons.why: A list of individual times can be long. A grouped table shows where they gather, but a careless boundary can count a value twice.

blocks.text: A class is a range of values. First record the variable and its unit, and find the smallest and largest valid observations. Choose a starting boundary no higher than the smallest value. Decide a width that produces enough detail for the question. For journey times, five-minute classes might make sense when the recorder measures in minutes. For annual rainfall totals, five minutes would be the wrong unit altogether. Classes must cover every valid value you are including.

A convenient rule is to include the lower endpoint and exclude the upper endpoint. Write “5 to under 10” rather than “5 to 10” if you want to make that explicit. Ten then belongs in “10 to under 15”. The notation $[5,10)$ means the same thing. A square bracket includes its endpoint, and a round bracket excludes it. These classes touch at 10 without overlapping. If you use 0 to under 20 as a total span, a maximum of exactly 20 needs another class or a clearly documented different final boundary. Do not quietly put that record wherever it fits your story.

For integer-valued data, labels such as 5–9 and 10–14 can be exhaustive with no gap in possible recorded integers. For a measured value like 9.7 those labels no longer describe complete classes. Use explicit boundary notation. Check that a new reader could place values at the boundary without asking you.

Use these invented wait times in minutes: 3, 4, 5, 7, 7, 10, 11, 14, 15, 18. Start at zero and use five-minute classes. Read each value and put one tally into its class. Here 5 belongs in the second class, 10 in the third and 15 in the fourth. The repeated 7 represents two waits and needs two tallies.

Check that the frequencies add to ten and that the unrounded proportions sum to one. A class with no waits should be shown as frequency zero if it is part of the declared span. A wait with unknown duration does not go in the zero class. Record unknown durations separately. You may report the distribution among valid times as long as you name that denominator and report how many records were excluded.

You can answer some questions exactly from the grouped table. Six of ten waits were at least five and under fifteen minutes. You cannot recover how many were exactly seven from the grouped table alone. You also cannot tell how many were under twelve because twelve is inside a class.

sections.title: Read what the table can show

blocks.text: The **class width** is the difference between its boundaries. For 10 to under 15 the width is five minutes. The **midpoint** is the average of the boundaries, here 12.5. It is a representative position for the class, not the observed average of the three waits inside it. Their real average is $(10+11+14)/3$, or about 11.67 minutes. When a table later uses midpoint estimates, keep that distinction visible.

Changing class width changes the detail that survives. Regrouping these waits into 0 to under 10 and 10 to under 20 gives five in each class. This clearer summary for a broad comparison hides the concentrations in the middle. Very narrow classes can preserve detail but leave many empty rows. If two groups will be compared, use the same boundaries so a difference in display cannot masquerade as a difference in measurements.

Open-ended classes such as “20 minutes or more” can be useful when only the threshold matters. That class has no known finite width or midpoint. Do not invent one and report it as exact. Always keep the raw records when privacy permits, so someone can retally at different boundaries or check an unusually long wait. If only grouped data were published, describe the class boundary and report the limit honestly.

warmup.answer: The number of observations in a value or category.

warmup.question: How do you find a relative frequency?
warmup.answer: Divide the class count by the eligible total.

summary: Classes must cover the valid observations without overlap.
Class width is upper minus lower; midpoint is halfway between.

lessons.title: Bar charts and pie charts
lessons.source: Statistics Canada · Statistics: Power from Data
lessons.goal: Choose a category display, draw bar lengths or sector angles and make group comparisons honestly.
lessons.why: A chart is a visual argument. When the display fits the question, readers can see the comparison without guessing which whole the numbers refer to.

blocks.text: For a bar chart, make one bar for each category. A bar's length represents its count or proportion. Use a common zero baseline when comparing lengths. Leave space between the bars to mark the separate categories. Put ordered categories such as low, medium and high in their meaningful order. For unordered categories, choose alphabetical order or sort by count if the question is which categories occur most often. Label the scale, the measure and the time window.

Consider an invented tally of 40 help requests classified by their main topic. The frequency table has 16 account requests, 12 connection requests, 8 payment requests and 4 other requests. A bar chart with counts on the vertical axis shows account as the longest bar and other as the shortest. Account is four times other because the lengths both begin at zero. If the vertical axis started at 3, the visible lengths would be 13 and 1. That would draw a far larger ratio than the counts support.

When you chart proportions, use a percentage scale and state the denominator. Four out of forty is 10 percent. A second week with six other requests could have a smaller percentage if the week had many more total requests. Counts describe work volume. Percentages describe the mix. Choose by the question and show both if readers need both answers.

spec.title: Help requests by main topic
spec.alt: Account has 16 requests, connection 12, payment 8 and other 4

blocks.text: A pie chart divides a circle into sectors. A sector's angle is its share of the total times 360 degrees. The four request categories account for 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%. Multiply each share as a decimal by 360. The angles are 144°, 108°, 72° and 36°. They add to 360°, which checks that the sectors can form one circle. To draw the pie by hand, use a protractor and start each sector where the previous one ends. Label with the category and its percentage, keeping the counts available in a table.

A pie chart requires nonnegative parts of one meaningful whole. Suppose each request can have several topics. One may count under account and payment. If the percentages are based on all requests, their sum can exceed 100%. This is a valid statement about topic prevalence, but it cannot be represented as parts of a single pie. Use bars for each topic's share and explain that a request can contribute to more than one bar.

Small sectors and close values are hard to compare by angle. When two shares are 24% and 26%, a reader often sees the difference more readily in bars sharing a baseline. A pie can work for a simple split when the question is whether a large share belongs to one or two categories. Show the date and whole group in either display.

Suppose a second invented week had 80 requests, of which 24 were account requests. The count rose from 16 to 24, a rise of eight requests. The share fell from 40% to 30%, a fall of ten percentage points. There is no contradiction. The denominator doubled, so account requests became a smaller part of the workload even as their number rose. Use two tables or adjacent bars for the comparison, with a shared scale. Say whether the group labels refer to weeks, teams or places.

When some categories are absent from a group, keep their positions if they are meaningful to the comparison. A measured zero deserves a zero-height bar or a labelled zero. A missing count deserves a missing marker, not a zero-height bar. Use readable labels rather than colour alone. Direct labels or a table below the chart make it possible to recover the important values without estimating heights.

Before sharing a display, ask another reader to identify the unit, denominator, largest category and claim. If they cannot tell whether 24 means requests or percent, revise the title and labels. If the graphic looks impressive because it uses perspective, three-dimensional slices or an unusual baseline, strip those away and see whether the evidence still supports the same sentence. The graphic should help readers check your claim.

lessons.title: Histograms
lessons.source: OpenStax · Histograms, frequency polygons and time series graphs
lessons.goal: Draw a histogram and use rectangle area to compare equal and unequal class widths.
lessons.why: The most common range of measurements is not always represented by the tallest count bar. When widths vary, interpreting a histogram correctly depends on area.

blocks.text: A histogram groups numerical values into intervals on a number line. Draw one rectangle over each interval. The width of the rectangle is the class width on the same continuous horizontal scale. Adjacent nonempty classes touch. An empty class has zero height and still occupies its horizontal span. This differs from a category bar chart, where the spaces and widths are mainly for layout. A histogram's interval order is fixed by the numerical values.

Use these invented waits in minutes: 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 17, 19. Mark boundaries at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20. Tally the four half-open intervals: 3, 4, 2, 3. For equal widths, count heights work because each area is the same multiple of its count. A class with twice the count has twice the area. Label that vertical axis “Frequency”. Under 10 minutes covers the first two rectangles, so seven of the twelve waits qualify.

The horizontal axis should show minutes, not just class names. Tick marks indicate where the boundaries fall. Look at the table while drawing and check that a boundary value such as 5 appears in only one rectangle. Describe the histogram as a picture of these observations. It is not enough evidence to know the exact probability of the next wait.

spec.title: Invented wait times
spec.alt: Four consecutive five-minute classes with counts 3, 4, 2 and 3

blocks.text: Now combine the last two classes into 10 to under 20. The frequencies are 3, 4 and 5, with widths 5, 5 and 10. If you use the counts as heights, the areas become 15, 20 and 50. The last class occupies a much larger share of ink than its five observations warrant. To avoid this, divide frequency by width. The resulting heights are 0.6, 0.8 and 0.5 observations per minute of class width. These heights are called **frequency densities**. The areas are 3, 4 and 5 again.

Notice that the widest class has the most observations but the smallest density. The middle interval has the greatest concentration per minute of class width. In the wide rectangle, the individual waits are not known to be evenly spread. The rectangle represents their count over a span. Multiply height by width to recover the count, and read the label carefully. If the vertical axis says relative frequency density instead, the area gives a proportion.

Scan from low to high. Ask where most observations lie, whether there are separated concentrations, and whether the values extend farther on one side. A **tail** is a thinner extension of the distribution beyond its main concentration. An isolated bin might represent a rare but valid event or a recording error. Look at the underlying values if you have them before deciding which. A histogram is a prompt for investigation.

Changing bins can smooth away a feature or make a small difference appear large. For a second view try shifting the starting boundary or using another reasonable width. If an apparent gap disappears, report that it depended on the grouping. For direct comparisons choose the same boundaries. When totals differ, draw relative frequency densities with the same scales, and state both valid counts. This compares shape rather than number of observations.

For a small list it may be easier to keep the raw values beside the histogram. A reader can then check that a wide interval contains several distinct waits. An open-ended class has no finite width. If a report only gives “20 or more,” keep that category in a table or recover a documented finite boundary before drawing a density rectangle.

lessons.title: Cumulative frequency and ogives
lessons.source: OpenStax · Histograms, frequency polygons and time series graphs
lessons.goal: Add running totals, draw an ogive and distinguish known threshold counts from interpolated estimates.
lessons.why: A queue manager often needs to know how many people waited less than a target time. Cumulative totals answer threshold questions directly.

blocks.text: A frequency table answers how many observations fell inside each class. A **cumulative frequency** answers how many fell below a class's upper boundary when the upper endpoint is excluded. Start with zero and add each class count in order. The first running total equals the first class count. The last equals the total number of valid measurements. A smaller cumulative count later in the list signals a mistake, since adding observations cannot reduce the count.

Use an invented service-time table in minutes. The intervals 0 to under 5, 5 to under 10, 10 to under 15 and 15 to under 20 have counts 3, 4, 2 and 3. The cumulative counts are 3, 7, 9 and 12. Seven services took less than ten minutes and nine took less than fifteen minutes. The difference 9 minus 7 gives two services at least ten and below fifteen minutes. Because our convention excludes upper boundaries, a service taking exactly ten minutes belongs to the difference, not the first seven.

To get cumulative percentages, divide each total by 12 and multiply by 100. The exact fractions are 3/12, 7/12, 9/12 and 12/12. Display them as 25%, about 58.3%, 75% and 100%. Calculate with the counts or unrounded fractions if you need a later difference. Small rounding changes do not mean the underlying count changed.

An **ogive** displays cumulative count or percentage against the upper class boundary. Mark the starting point (0, 0) because no valid service time was below the starting boundary in this table. Then plot (5, 3), (10, 7), (15, 9) and (20, 12). Connect successive points by straight segments for a grouped-data ogive. The segments do not assert that observations actually occurred uniformly within each interval. They show a simple way to estimate what might be between known points.

The axes should say “Upper time boundary in minutes” and “Services with time below boundary.” If you plot percentages, replace the count label and finish at 100%. A horizontal segment means there were no observations in that class. A steeper segment means the count accumulated faster over that range. Do not compare slopes from two ogives if one uses counts and the other percentages without checking the denominators.

There is also an exact display when raw values are available. An empirical cumulative distribution can jump at each recorded value. One common version reports the share at or below each value. That inclusive rule differs from our grouped points at an exclusive upper boundary. State which rule you are using, particularly when many observations land exactly on a threshold.

spec.title: Cumulative service count
spec.alt: The cumulative count increases from zero to twelve through three, seven and nine
spec.note: Invented practice counts; straight segments interpolate between class boundaries

blocks.text: At 12.5 minutes you are halfway from 10 to 15. The line rises from 7 to 9 over that span, so linear interpolation gives 8 below 12.5. This is an estimate. The two observations in the class might both be below 12.5, both above it, or one on either side. All of those raw lists produce the same grouped table. The exact count below 12.5 is bounded between 7 and 9. The chart cannot recover the individual times.

You can also read the graph in reverse. To find an estimated middle threshold, find half the observations on the vertical axis, here 6. Six lies between the cumulative counts 3 and 7. It is three quarters of the way across that vertical rise. Three quarters of the five-minute class width is 3.75 minutes. The estimated halfway time is 8.75 minutes. The raw data could give a different median. You will work out exact medians from raw lists later.

Use the right tool for the decision. If a public target is defined as “less than 12.5 minutes,” ask for raw times or a table with a boundary at 12.5 when the decision hinges on a single case. If all you need is a broad picture, a labelled estimate may be sufficient. State the assumption and keep the observed boundary totals available.

lessons.title: Stem-and-leaf plots
lessons.source: Statistics Canada · Statistics: Power from Data
lessons.goal: Build a stem-and-leaf plot, read its key and recover every recorded value.
lessons.why: For a small data set, a stem-and-leaf plot shows the distribution while preserving individual observations. You can check an unusual point without reopening the raw file.

blocks.text: In a stem-and-leaf plot, part of each value becomes the **stem** and the remaining digit becomes a **leaf**. Use the same split throughout. For whole minutes, let the tens digit be the stem and the ones digit be the leaf. Then 27 minutes becomes stem 2, leaf 7. The **key** shows how to read a pair. Write “2 | 7 means 27 minutes.” A stem and leaf without a key can be ambiguous. The same symbols might mean 2.7 seconds in a different display.

Use these invented journey times, in minutes: 12, 18, 21, 25, 25, 27, 31, 36, 42, 48 and 53. Start with stems 1 through 5, one per line. Read each observation and place its leaf on the right stem. Keep every repetition. Both observations of 25 have the same stem and leaf, so write two leaves of 5. Sorting the leaves within each row helps readers see the smallest and largest values. A finished row for the twenties is “2 | 1 5 5 7”.

Some datasets need more than one digit in the stem. For 124, a stem of 12 and leaf of 4 is possible. For measurements recorded to a tenth, a stem of 12 and leaf of 4 could instead mean 12.4. The key must specify both scale and units. Use a leaf digit of zero when the last place is zero. Omitting zero would remove an actual value.

sections.title: Recover values and inspect the shape

blocks.text: Read the stems in order, and the leaves in order within each row. The worked example is:

The number of leaves is 2 + 4 + 2 + 2 + 1, or eleven. That is a useful check against the original record. The shortest recorded journey is 12 minutes and the longest 53. Four trips were at least 20 and below 30 minutes. In the same row, three of those were at least 25, since the leaves are 5, 5 and 7. A grouped table would tell us there were four trips in their twenties without showing those details.

If the range skips a stem, include a blank row where the numeric scale needs it. A plot with times 12, 15, 41 and 42 should show the empty twenties and thirties. Otherwise a reader may think the two concentrations touch. Blank stems mean no included observations there. They do not represent unknown journey times. Record missing values outside the display.

A long row shows more observations in that span. Do not infer that all times in the row are equally likely. Inspect the leaves. Some can repeat while others are absent. A plot of one week shows what was recorded that week, and it takes a sound sampling plan to generalise beyond it.

sections.title: Choose a scale that suits the data

blocks.text: If a row is crowded, split each stem into two rows: leaves 0 to 4, then leaves 5 to 9. Label the convention so nobody thinks you repeated data. For the twenties, the first row contains leaf 1 and the second contains 5, 5 and 7. The measurement values have not changed, only the display. Splitting every stem consistently keeps rows comparable.

You can also make a back-to-back display for two small groups by placing one group's leaves left of the stems and the other group's leaves right of them. Both sides must share the same units and key. Count the records in each group before comparing row lengths. A group with twice as many records may produce longer rows even when its distribution has much the same shape. For a size-independent comparison use proportions or separate histograms on a common scale.

With thousands of rows a stem plot becomes hard to read, and with many digits you may have to round before drawing it. State any rounding because you can then recover only the rounded values. Where precision is important, keep the original table and use a plot for the broad pattern. Choose the least complicated display that still answers the question.

lessons.title: Charts that mislead
lessons.source: Statistics Canada · Statistics: Power from Data
lessons.goal: Audit a chart's scale, categories, denominator and time window, then redraw it to support a checkable claim.
lessons.why: A chart can contain accurate numbers while leading readers toward a wrong comparison. You can diagnose the problem by reconstructing what its marks mean.

blocks.text: Start by reading what a mark represents. A bar represents magnitude by length. A line shows the movement of values along an ordered scale, often time. A histogram uses the area of rectangles to represent frequency when scaled by density. If you mistake one encoding for another, the same picture can suggest an entirely different result. Find the units and identify the start of each scale before interpreting it.

Suppose an invented report shows counts of 98 and 100 with the vertical axis starting at 97. The visible bar lengths are 1 and 3, so one appears three times the other. The actual ratio is 100/98, only about 1.02. Redraw the bars from zero, or show a table of the exact counts. A zoomed line chart can be useful for small movements when the axis is clearly labelled and the context explains their size. The problem is drawing a length comparison with an undisclosed or inappropriate baseline.

Pictures can mislead by area too. If a pictured parcel has twice the height and twice the width, it covers four times the area. Readers may perceive four times the quantity when the data only doubled. Use simple marks or direct numeric labels, and avoid perspective that makes the front of a chart look larger.

Consider an invented clinic example. Last year 20 of 100 eligible visits were late. This year 30 of 200 were late. The count increased by ten. The proportion fell from 20% to 15%. A caption that says “late visits rose by half” could be correct for counts, but it would mislead readers if the claim is that visits became more likely to be late. Compute both and state the denominator, eligibility and period.

Compare the definitions next. If one clinic calls a visit late after five minutes and another after ten, bars with matching axes do not repair the difference. Likewise, a figure that covers a full month cannot be compared directly to a week as if the exposure were identical. Find comparable definitions, calculate a rate when it answers the question, or keep the numbers separate with a warning about comparability.

Time windows can change the impression. A chart that begins just before an unusually low value may look like strong growth even if the longer series is flat. Look for omitted years and check whether gaps are equally spaced. Missing years should not be plotted as zero. If you connect observations across a gap, make clear that the values between the observations are unknown. If a report has been rebased or revised, check the producer's documentation before joining values into one line.

Write down the exact sentence the graphic appears to support. Then record its source table, dates, units, denominator and exclusions. If you cannot locate an original table, say what is unknown instead of guessing. Try reconstructing at least two points by hand from the numbers. If the figure uses percentages, verify whether a difference is in percentage points or a percentage change relative to a baseline.

Now choose a chart that matches the question. For counts across categories, use bars from zero. For a time series, keep the chronological scale honest, show the units and annotate a definition change. For grouped measurements, keep the interval widths meaningful. Whenever comparisons involve two charts, use compatible scales and units. Include a short caption with the measured difference and the populations it refers to.

Finally, ask what the chart still cannot establish. It may show that a drop happened near the launch of a new policy. A plot alone does not demonstrate that the policy caused it. It may also show an apparent change driven by a small number of cases. Keep the evidence and its limits together. A reader should be able to reproduce the reported comparison and see what would change the conclusion.

lessons.title: Averages and spread, worked by hand
lessons.source: OpenStax · Introductory Statistics 2e · Sections 2.5 to 2.7
lessons.goal: Calculate the mean, median, mode, range, quartiles, variance and standard deviation by hand, choose the right average for the data, and say what each number means in words.
lessons.why: An average describes where values sit. It can hide how widely they vary. A measure of spread helps you compare groups with the same average and spot values worth checking.

blocks.text: An average is one number that represents a typical value. There are three main ones, and they answer different questions. We'll use this invented data: the weekly study hours of 7 students.
The mean
The **mean** adds everything up, and divides by how many there are. In symbols, the sample mean is written x-bar, and the number of values is n.
The median
The **median** is the middle value once the data are **in order**. With n values, its position is (n + 1) / 2. Here (7 + 1) / 2 = 4, so it's the 4th value: **8**.
With an even number of values, take the mean of the middle two. For 4, 6, 8, 10, the median is (6 + 8) / 2 = 7.
Taking the middle value without ordering the data first. For 9, 2, 7 the median is 7, not 2.
The mode
The **mode** is the most common value. Here it's **6**. Data can have no mode, or several. The mode is the only average that works for nominal data such as "most common state".
Which to use
The mean is 10, the median is 8 and the mode is 6. They differ because one student's 26 hours pulls the mean up. Six of seven students are below 12, and the mean is above most of them.

head: Situation
Best average
Why
rows: Roughly symmetric, with no extreme values
Skewed, or with outliers, such as incomes
One extreme value barely affects it
The only one that makes sense

blocks.text: A useful guide: in right-skewed data, the mean is usually above the median. That's why "average salary" often sounds higher than what a typical person earns.

blocks.question: 5 workers earn N50k, N60k, N60k, N70k and N1,000k per month. What are the mean and median, and which describes a typical worker better?
blocks.answer: The mean is 1,240 / 5 = N248k. The median is N60k. The median is the better description, as the mean is above four of the five workers.

blocks.text: Two classes can have the same mean and be nothing alike.
**Spread**, also called **dispersion**, measures how far values vary.
Range
The **range** is the largest minus the smallest. Class A's is 2, and Class B's is 80. It's simple, but it depends on just two values, so one outlier changes it completely.
Quartiles and the interquartile range

**Quartiles** mark positions about a quarter, halfway and three quarters through ordered data. The halfway value Q2 is the median. The **interquartile range** is IQR = Q3 - Q1. It describes central spread and is usually less sensitive to extreme values than the overall range.

For 4, 6, 6, 8, 9, 11, 26: the median is 8, so the lower half is 4, 6, 6 and the upper half is 9, 11, 26. Q1 = 6, Q3 = 11, and IQR = 5. Textbooks have slightly different rules for finding quartiles, so use your course's. A common rule for spotting outliers flags anything above Q3 + 1.5 x IQR, here 11 + 7.5 = 18.5, so 26 counts as an outlier.
Variance and standard deviation
These measure how far values typically are from the mean. They use all the data.
The **variance** averages the squared distances from the mean. For a sample, you divide by n - 1. The **standard deviation** (SD) is its square root, which puts it back in the original units.

blocks.code:
sample variance  s^2 = sum of (value - mean)^2 / (n - 1)
standard deviation s = square root of s^2

blocks.text: Worked example: standard deviation by hand
Data: 2, 4, 4, 6, 9. Here n = 5, and the mean is 25 / 5 = 5.
Variance = 28 / (5 - 1) = 7. Standard deviation = square root of 7, which is about **2.65**.
Notice that the middle column sums to 0, and it always does. That's why you square: otherwise the positives and negatives would cancel out, and that sum is also a handy check on your arithmetic.

Divide by n - 1 for a **sample**, and by n when you truly have the whole **population**. Dividing by n - 1 corrects for the tendency of a sample to underestimate the population's spread. Check which your question wants, as exam questions and calculators both have both forms.
Python's `statistics` module confirms the work:

blocks.code:
import statistics
data = [2, 4, 4, 6, 9]
print(statistics.mean(data))
print(statistics.median(data))
print(statistics.mode(data))
print(statistics.variance(data))
print(round(statistics.stdev(data), 2))

sections.title: What a standard deviation tells you

blocks.text: A larger SD means larger squared deviations from the mean on average, under the same calculation. In a normal distribution, the **empirical rule** gives about 68% within 1 SD of the mean, 95% within 2 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD. For data with a roughly normal shape these are guides. Check actual counts if you need an observed share.
Move the sliders to see it. The mean moves the bell left and right, and the standard deviation makes it wider or narrower.

spec.alt: A bell-shaped curve. A slider for the mean moves it left and right, and a slider for the standard deviation makes it wider and flatter, or narrower and taller.

blocks.text: So if scores have a mean of 60 and an SD of 10, a score of 62 is ordinary, while 95 is very unusual. A **z-score** says how many SDs a value is from the mean: z = (value - mean) / SD. So 95 has a z-score of (95 - 60) / 10 = 3.5.

This is basically how simple fraud rules work. If an account usually spends a mean of N10,000 with an SD of N3,000, then a N70,000 transaction has z = 20, which is worth a closer look. Real systems are more complicated, partly since spending data is often strongly skewed, and the rule above only applies to bell-shaped data.
Exams often give a frequency table, not raw values. You can't know the exact values, so use each class's midpoint as an estimate.
Worked example: mean of grouped data

Mean = sum of (f x x) / sum of f = 255 / 10 = **25.5**. The result is an estimate, since we're assuming that values sit at the midpoints. Your course will also show formulas for the median and SD of grouped data.

lessons.title: The median and quartiles
lessons.source: OpenStax · Measures of the spread of the data
lessons.goal: Find the median and quartiles from ordered data and report the convention behind the interquartile range.
lessons.why: A single typical value can hide how tightly values cluster. Quartiles locate the middle of the ordered observations without relying on the largest values.

blocks.text: Follow one long wait through the mean, median and quartiles. Pause to predict what each summary will do.

The median is a centre based on position. Sort observations from smallest to largest before calculating it. Preserve repeats. Each observation has its own position, even if several share a value. For an odd number of values, the median is the observation with equal numbers of positions on either side. For an even number of numeric values, use the arithmetic mean of the middle two. These rules describe positions in the ordered list. A median is not required to appear as an observed value.

Take these invented wait times in minutes, in arrival order: 22, 8, 14, 7, 35, 14, 10. The sorted list is 7, 8, 10, 14, 14, 22, 35. There are seven observations, so the fourth is the median: 14 minutes. If the final value were 135 instead of 35, the median would remain 14 because the middle position would still hold the same value. The mean and range would change. This is why medians are often useful when a few recorded values are very large.

For eight ordered waits 4, 6, 7, 9, 13, 14, 18, 20, the fourth and fifth values are 9 and 13. Their mean is 11. No observation has to equal 11. Read the result in minutes and keep the sample size next to it. If the observations are only ordinal labels such as “slow, medium, fast”, report the middle categories as appropriate. Do not average the codes for two labels as if the steps between them were equal.

The median divides the ordered list in half. Quartiles give positions about a quarter and three quarters through. Several established algorithms give slightly different quartiles, especially on small datasets. In this course we use the **median of halves excluding the overall median**. With an odd list, set aside the middle observation before taking the lower and upper halves. With an even list, split the list into two equal halves. Find each half's median by the same middle rule. Call them Q1 and Q3. The overall median is Q2.

For the seven sorted waits, remove position four from the halves but leave its equal-valued neighbour in the upper half. The lower half is 7, 8, 10. Its median is 8. The upper half is 14, 22, 35. Its median is 22. Q1 is 8 and Q3 is 22. For the eight waits, the lower half is 4, 6, 7, 9, so Q1 is 6.5. The upper half is 13, 14, 18, 20, so Q3 is 16. Ties and interpolation mean the cut points need not divide the data into four piles with exactly the same numbers of distinct values.

When a spreadsheet gives a different result, check its algorithm before changing your answer. A tool might interpolate using positions based on the full list. That is another definition, not evidence of a broken calculator. Use the same method across groups and state it alongside the result.

The **interquartile range**, or IQR, is Q3 minus Q1. It measures the width of the middle part of the distribution in the original units. The seven waits have IQR 22 − 8 = 14 minutes. Their overall range is 35 − 7 = 28 minutes. When the maximum changes to 135, the overall range becomes 128 minutes, while this IQR stays 14. Quartiles are less sensitive to extreme values, but moving observations through their positions can still change them.

An IQR of zero does not prove all observations are equal. For 1, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 9, both half medians are 5, while the endpoints differ. Report the median and quartiles together, or use a five-number summary if the ends matter. Do not claim that exactly half the observations lie strictly between Q1 and Q3; ties can put several on the boundaries.

If you only have grouped counts, the ogive can suggest quartile positions by reading near 25% and 75%. Those readings use interpolation and should be labelled estimates. Use raw ordered observations when an exact answer under your chosen rule matters.

warmup.answer: Subtract the minimum from the maximum.

lessons.title: Variance and standard deviation
lessons.source: OpenStax · Measures of the spread of the data
lessons.goal: Calculate deviations, population and sample variance, and standard deviation. Explain their units and denominators.
lessons.why: Two groups can have the same mean but different consistency. Standard deviation describes spread around the mean and makes that difference visible.

blocks.text: A deviation is a recorded value minus its mean. It is a signed difference, so values below the mean have negative deviations. Take three invented waiting times of 2, 4 and 6 minutes. Their mean is 4 and their deviations are −2, 0 and 2 minutes. Those deviations sum to zero. This is true for any list if you subtract its own exact arithmetic mean, because the total of all values equals the mean times their count. Simply averaging the signed differences will always give zero, even for widely spread data.

Squaring the deviations prevents negative and positive differences from cancelling. Here their squares are 4, 0 and 4 square minutes, giving a sum of squares of 8. Squaring also puts more weight on distant observations: a deviation of 4 contributes four times as much as a deviation of 2. Keep this sensitivity in mind when the data include unusually large values.

Work in a small table with a value, its deviation and its squared deviation on each row. Use the unrounded mean for the deviation calculation. Round only after the final step. If your signed deviations do not add to zero apart from small rounding error, check the arithmetic before continuing.

When the list is the whole population of interest, divide the sum of squared deviations by the number of values. The result is the **population variance**. For the three waits that is 8/3 square minutes. The **population standard deviation** is the nonnegative square root, about 1.63 minutes. The square root returns the unit to minutes. A variance does not have the original unit, which is why “a variance of 2.67 minutes” is incorrect.

For a sample used to estimate the population variance, the usual **sample variance** divides by one fewer than the sample size. Here 8/(3−1) = 4 square minutes, so the sample standard deviation is 2 minutes. State which calculation you used. When the population mean is unknown and you fit the sample mean, it sits as close as possible to those sampled points in the squared sense. Under ordinary independent, identically distributed sampling with finite variance, dividing by n−1 corrects the downward bias of the variance estimator. The sample standard deviation itself is not in general unbiased. A sample with one observation does not support this sample variance rule.

For a census of all three waits that matter to a question, the population formula is suitable. If those are three randomly drawn waits used to estimate variability across a larger system, the sample formula may be suitable. A label such as “sample” should follow the study question and design, not just the number of rows.

Compare the invented lists 3, 4, 5 and 1, 4, 7. Both have mean 4. In the first, deviations are −1, 0 and 1. In the second they are −3, 0 and 3. The second set's standard deviation is three times the first under either denominator, while the variance is nine times as large. Adding the same constant to every value would shift the mean and each value together, leaving their deviations unchanged. Converting minutes to seconds multiplies each deviation and the standard deviation by 60, and variance by 3600.

A standard deviation of zero means all included values are equal. A large standard deviation can arise from broad variation or a few extremes. Use a chart and compare with the IQR before claiming that most values are widely spread. A universal rule such as “about two thirds are within one standard deviation” does not follow from the definition. That familiar rule is an approximation for a particular distribution shape, not a guarantee for arbitrary data.
Python's standard library can check your hand calculation. The two functions here differ by the denominator just described.

waits = [2, 4, 6]
print(round(pstdev(waits), 2))
print(round(stdev(waits), 2))
