questions.feedback: It was calculated from a sample, so it's a statistic that estimates the parameter.
choices: A parameter of all the customers
A statistic
A population of late payers

questions.question: What is the equal-chance property of a simple random sample?
answers: Each member has the same individual selection probability
questions.feedback: Randomness guards against favouring anyone. It doesn't guarantee a perfect match.
choices: The sample will be large enough to trust
Each member has the same individual selection probability
The sample will match the population exactly

questions.question: Doubling the size of a biased sample does what to its bias?
answers: Leaves the bias in place
questions.feedback: More of the same kind of data keeps the same distortion. It only reduces chance error.
choices: Removes the bias, given enough data
Cuts the bias in half, as you'd expect
Leaves the bias in place

questions.question: A radio station asks listeners to text in their view. What kind of sample is this?
answers: Self-selected
questions.feedback: The listeners decide whether to respond. People who feel strongly are more likely to.
choices: Simple random
Self-selected
Stratified

questions.question: You split students by level, and then randomly sample within each level. What's this design called?
answers: Stratified sampling
questions.feedback: Stratified sampling divides the population into groups and samples randomly within each.
choices: Stratified sampling
Convenience sampling
Survivorship sampling

questions.question: Why do different random samples from the same population give different statistics?
answers: Because of natural sampling variability
questions.feedback: Chance alone makes samples differ. A larger sample reduces this.
questions.part: What a sample can and cannot tell you
choices: Because at least one of them must be biased
Because the population changes every time
Because of natural sampling variability

questions.question: A course on making money online shows 10 students who now earn well. What should you ask first?
answers: How many took the course in total, and what happened to the rest
questions.feedback: This is survivorship. You're shown winners. The base, including those who failed, is what you need.
choices: Whether those 10 people look trustworthy on camera
How many took the course in total, and what happened to the rest
Whether the course has a good website and logo

questions.question: A fraud model is trained only on transactions already flagged by human reviewers. What's the sampling risk?
answers: It only learns from what reviewers noticed, so fraud they missed stays invisible
questions.feedback: The sample misses cases nobody flagged, which is undercoverage. It matters a great deal in real fraud work.
choices: It only learns from what reviewers noticed, so fraud they missed stays invisible
The model can't work because it uses numbers from a real bank
There's no risk, since humans reviewed every one of the transactions

questions.question: A university asks graduates to report their salaries. Those with good jobs reply far more often. How will the average reported salary compare with the true average?
answers: It will probably be too high
questions.feedback: This is non-response bias. Those with low pay are underrepresented, which pushes the average up.
choices: It will be about the same, thanks to a large mailing list
It will probably be too high
It will probably be too low

cards: What's the difference between a population and a sample?
The population is the whole group of interest. The sample is the part actually observed.
What's the difference between a parameter and a statistic?
A parameter describes the population. A statistic is calculated from the sample and estimates it.
Does a larger sample remove bias?
No. It reduces chance error, but not errors from how the sample was chosen.
What's survivorship bias?
Drawing conclusions only from those who lasted or succeeded, while those who failed are invisible.
What's a simple random sample?
Every member has the same chance, and every group of that size is equally likely.

questions.question: You study the duration of each bus journey. What should one row represent?
answers: One journey with a defined start and end
questions.feedback: The question is about individual journeys.
choices: One journey with a defined start and end
One passenger regardless of journey count
One route regardless of journeys taken

questions.question: You set a threshold of at most ten minutes late. Which observation qualifies?
answers: An arrival exactly ten minutes late
questions.feedback: At most includes equality.
choices: An arrival exactly ten minutes late
An arrival eleven minutes late
An arrival twelve minutes late

questions.question: Why fix eligibility before recording results?
answers: So inclusion does not depend on the result
questions.feedback: An outcome-dependent inclusion rule can distort the result.
choices: So inclusion does not depend on the result
So the sample always includes everybody
So every recorded value must be positive

questions.question: Which asks about one measurable thing?
answers: How many minutes was your last trip?
questions.feedback: The first gives a unit and a time reference.
choices: How many minutes was your last trip?
Was your last trip cheap and quick?
How much better was the last trip?

questions.question: What is a pilot for?
answers: Finding unclear rules before full collection
questions.feedback: Pilot cases test whether the collection works.
choices: Finding unclear rules before full collection
Quietly removing unusually slow observations
Replacing the need to document the main survey

questions.question: An empty log cell means a time is unknown. What should you store?
answers: A documented missing value, with reason if known
questions.feedback: Unknown is not an observed number.
choices: A documented missing value, with reason if known
A zero so all rows are easy to calculate
The average time from the other rows

questions.question: A receipt proves 540 was entered instead of 450. How do you fix it?
answers: Keep the original and record the correction with its evidence
questions.feedback: A traceable correction preserves the evidence.
choices: Keep the original and record the correction with its evidence
Overwrite the entry and remove the old copy immediately
Drop the row because a value once looked odd

questions.question: In an invented log, six sessions have known starts and five were on time. What is the proportion among known starts? Enter a simplified fraction like 2/3.
questions.feedback: Five qualifying starts out of six known starts.

questions.question: A form asks if a service is fast and affordable. How would you improve it?
answers: Use separate questions for speed and affordability
questions.feedback: Speed and cost can give different answers.
choices: Use separate questions for speed and affordability
Ask the same combined question twice for reliability
Replace both questions with whether it was excellent

questions.question: A traffic sensor is offline for one hour. What should that hour count as?
answers: Missing, unless another source confirms the count
questions.feedback: No recording does not mean no traffic.
choices: Missing, unless another source confirms the count
Zero, since the sensor saved no cars
The average of the previous two hours

questions.question: You compare morning and afternoon starts. How should a 09:00 booking that began at 13:00 be grouped under the lesson's rule?
answers: Morning, with its actual start and delay recorded
questions.feedback: The planned time defines the comparison groups.
choices: Morning, with its actual start and delay recorded
Afternoon, because that is when it began
Neither, because scheduled and actual times differ

cards: What is a pilot?
A small trial to find and fix collection problems before the main round.
When is a blank different from zero?
A blank records an unknown or inapplicable value. Zero is an observed value.
What belongs in a correction log?
Original value, replacement value and evidence for the change.

questions.question: What distinguishes a census by design?
answers: It attempts to cover every eligible unit
questions.feedback: A census aims for complete coverage, although actual coverage can differ.
choices: It attempts to cover every eligible unit
It selects an equal number in each district
It records whoever visits a service office

questions.question: Which is an administrative record?
answers: Birth registrations logged by a registry
questions.feedback: Registration records are produced through a service.
choices: Birth registrations logged by a registry
Interviews with a sampled set of households
A count conducted by visiting every dwelling

questions.question: Why might a survey's published share differ from its raw row share?
answers: The estimate can use sampling weights and eligibility rules
questions.feedback: Published estimates follow the survey's documented method.
choices: The estimate can use sampling weights and eligibility rules
A share is calculated without any denominator
Each published share must equal the raw number of rows

questions.question: A report released in May describes January to March. What is the reference period?
answers: January to March, the period described
questions.feedback: Release and reference dates are separate fields.
questions.part: Read the release beside the number
choices: January to March, the period described
May, the month the report appeared
The date you downloaded the document

questions.question: A percentage is reported without the eligible population. What should you find?
answers: The denominator definition in the metadata
questions.feedback: The denominator tells you whom the proportion describes.
questions.part: Read the release beside the number
choices: The denominator definition in the metadata
The first date the web page was visited
A second percentage of a different population

questions.question: What can you infer from the name 'poverty measure' alone?
answers: Too little to know the rules used to classify people
questions.feedback: Read the metadata for the definition.
questions.part: Read the release beside the number
choices: Too little to know the rules used to classify people
That the measure always uses a fixed income threshold
That two releases using that word must have the same method

questions.question: Why preserve the publication version?
answers: Later releases may revise values or definitions
questions.feedback: Versions let readers reconstruct the original comparison.
choices: Later releases may revise values or definitions
The publication month sets the denominator size
Every revision makes the earlier release fraudulent

questions.question: What is the first check when combining two series?
answers: The measures, units, dates and populations are comparable
questions.feedback: Matching structure cannot substitute for comparable definitions.
choices: The measures, units, dates and populations are comparable
Both tables have the same number of columns
Both reports have the same heading font

questions.question: Two releases report different estimates for the same period. How should you proceed?
answers: Find the reason, select a version and document it
questions.feedback: A revision can reflect a changed method or new information.
choices: Find the reason, select a version and document it
Average the two numbers and discard their dates
Use the higher estimate since it contains more information

questions.question: A registry processes 240 certificates in April. Can you treat that as the number of births in April?
answers: Only if the records identify the same birth period and coverage
questions.feedback: Processing dates can differ from dates of birth.
choices: Only if the records identify the same birth period and coverage
Yes, because both records are about births
Yes, provided the certificates all have a processing date

questions.question: A screenshot shows an official number with no period or geography. What should you do before quoting it?
answers: Locate the original table and copy the missing context
questions.feedback: The value needs traceable context.
questions.part: Read the release beside the number
choices: Locate the original table and copy the missing context
Assume it refers to the most recent national quarter
Estimate its period from the colour of the graph

cards: What is the reference period?
The time the observation describes.
Why may survey file counts differ from published estimates?
The published estimate may use survey weights and eligibility rules.
Why keep the release version?
A later release can revise a value or change its method.

questions.question: 12 of 60 students chose Card. What's the relative frequency?
questions.feedback: 12 divided by 60 is 0.2.
questions.part: From raw data to a frequency table

questions.question: Classes run 10 to 19, 20 to 29 and 30 to 39, with frequencies 4, 7 and 9. What's the cumulative frequency up to 29?
What's the midpoint of the class 20 to 29?
Which chart suits a numerical variable such as exam scores?
answers: A histogram
questions.feedback: A histogram shows how numerical values are distributed.
choices: A pie chart
A histogram
A bar chart of names

questions.question: What separates a histogram from a bar chart?
answers: A histogram has a number scale, and its bars touch
questions.feedback: Bar charts have separate categories that could be reordered.
choices: A histogram has a number scale, and its bars touch
A histogram can only ever be drawn by a computer
A bar chart can only ever show a percentage value

questions.question: Most incomes are moderate, and a few are huge. What shape is that?
answers: Right-skewed
questions.feedback: The long tail points toward the high values.
choices: Left-skewed
Symmetric
Right-skewed

questions.question: Why can't classes overlap, as in 10 to 20 and 20 to 30?
answers: A value of 20 would fit in two classes
questions.feedback: Each value must fall in exactly one class.
choices: Because the chart wouldn't look as good when drawn
A value of 20 would fit in two classes
Because classes must always be of an odd width

questions.question: A histogram has two clear peaks. What might that suggest?
answers: Two different groups may be mixed in the data
questions.feedback: Two peaks are often a sign of two groups, such as day and evening students.
choices: Two different groups may be mixed in the data
The data must have been entered wrongly
The average has been calculated wrongly

questions.question: Transaction amounts on an account are nearly all under N20,000, with one of N4,800,000. What should an analyst do?
answers: Investigate it, since it could be an error or actual fraud
questions.feedback: Outliers need explaining. In fraud work, they can be the whole point.
choices: Delete it, as it spoils the shape of the chart
Investigate it, since it could be an error or actual fraud
Ignore it, as one value can't make any real difference

questions.question: A politician's bar chart shows a rise from 40% to 42%, and the axis runs from 39% to 43%. The bars look very different. What's the honest description?
answers: A 2-point rise, made to look bigger by a cut axis
questions.feedback: Read the numbers and not the picture. Bars should normally start at zero.
choices: A huge rise, as can be seen from the height of the bars
A 2-point rise, made to look bigger by a cut axis
No change at all, since charts can't show percentages

questions.question: You want to show how your monthly spending changed over a year. Which chart suits it best?
answers: A line chart with months along the bottom
questions.feedback: Change over time is what a line chart is for.
choices: A line chart with months along the bottom
A pie chart with one slice for each month
A histogram with a bar for each amount spent

cards: What's relative frequency?
A category's frequency divided by the total number of cases.
What's cumulative frequency?
A running total of frequencies, up to and including that class.
Bar chart or histogram: what's the difference?
Bar charts show separate categories. Histograms show a numerical scale, and their bars touch.
What four things do you look for in a distribution?
Centre, spread, shape and outliers.
What does right-skewed mean?
A long tail toward the high values, as with incomes.
What's a common way a bar chart misleads?
Its axis doesn't start at zero, so small differences look huge.

questions.question: Where does 10 belong in [5,10) and [10,15)?
answers: [10,15), the class starting at 10
questions.feedback: The upper endpoint is excluded.
choices: [10,15), the class starting at 10
[5,10), the class ending at 10
Both classes, since both show 10

questions.question: What is the width of [12,18)?
answers: six
questions.feedback: Subtract 12 from 18.

questions.question: What is wrong with [0,10) and [8,20)?
answers: Values from 8 to below 10 fit twice
questions.feedback: The intervals overlap.
choices: Values from 8 to below 10 fit twice
Values from 8 to below 10 fit nowhere
Every value belongs to exactly one class

questions.question: The valid count is 20, and a class contains 6. Give its relative frequency as a decimal.
questions.feedback: Six divided by 20 is 0.30.

questions.question: What should the class frequencies sum to?
answers: The number of valid included observations
questions.feedback: Every eligible observation contributes one tally.
choices: The number of valid included observations
The sum of all recorded measurement values
The midpoint of the longest observed wait

questions.question: Where does an unknown wait time belong?
answers: In the separate missing count
questions.feedback: Unknown is not a measurement of zero.
choices: In the separate missing count
In the class that starts at zero
In the middle of the fullest class

questions.question: What is the midpoint of [10,15)?
questions.feedback: Add the boundaries and divide by two.
questions.part: Read what the table can show

questions.question: What is lost when only a grouped table is saved?
answers: The exact values within each class
questions.feedback: Class counts do not store individual measurements.
questions.part: Read what the table can show
choices: The exact values within each class
The total number of valid records
The count for each listed interval

questions.question: Two clinics use different wait-time boundaries. What improves their comparison?
answers: Retally both with the same class boundaries
questions.feedback: Shared classes compare the same spans.
questions.part: Read what the table can show
choices: Retally both with the same class boundaries
Compare the third row regardless of its limits
Divide each class count by the other clinic's total

questions.question: A dashboard lists 12 orders at 0 to under 5 days and 8 at 5 to under 10. How many took under 10 days?
answers: twenty
questions.feedback: Both whole classes lie under ten.

questions.question: A table ends with a class called 30 or more. Can you get its midpoint from that label?
answers: No, because its upper boundary is unknown
questions.feedback: An open class lacks a finite upper boundary.
questions.part: Read what the table can show
choices: No, because its upper boundary is unknown
Yes, because 30 is its only possible value
Yes, because the midpoint is always 30 plus 5

cards: What does [5,10) include?
5 and values below 10, but not 10.
How wide is [10,15)?
5 units.
Is the class midpoint the observed mean?
No. It is halfway between boundaries.

questions.question: What is the usual starting point for bars that compare amounts?
answers: Zero on the common magnitude scale
questions.feedback: A zero baseline preserves the meaning of lengths.
choices: Zero on the common magnitude scale
The smallest observed amount in each group
A different baseline chosen for each bar

questions.question: How should low, medium and high usually appear?
answers: In their meaningful low-to-high order
questions.feedback: They are ordered categories.
choices: In their meaningful low-to-high order
Sorted alphabetically as unrelated labels
In a random order for each group

questions.question: What does a bar labelled 20% need beside it?
answers: The group or denominator it describes
questions.feedback: The share only makes sense relative to a whole.
choices: The group or denominator it describes
A different colour for every screen
The mean of the category labels

questions.question: What angle represents 25% of a pie? Enter degrees as a number.
questions.feedback: One quarter of 360° is 90°.

questions.question: What should the angles of all slices sum to? Enter degrees as a number.
questions.feedback: The slices complete one circle.

questions.question: What does a 36° sector represent? Give a percentage.
answers: 10 percent
questions.feedback: 36 divided by 360 is 0.10.

questions.question: A count rises while its share falls. How can this happen?
answers: The overall total grows faster than the count
questions.feedback: A growing denominator can shrink a share.
choices: The overall total grows faster than the count
The overall total must stay the same
The category must have been removed from the total

questions.question: What should a missing group count look like?
answers: A missing marker rather than a measured zero
questions.feedback: Missing and zero convey different information.
choices: A missing marker rather than a measured zero
A zero bar to keep the chart orderly
A bar equal to the median of other groups

questions.question: Residents choose every transport mode they used. What is an appropriate display?
answers: Separate bars with a note that multiple responses are allowed
questions.feedback: Overlapping categories need not sum to one whole.
choices: Separate bars with a note that multiple responses are allowed
A pie treating the shares as mutually exclusive
A pie dropping any response that makes the total too large

questions.question: Two charts of clinic visits are intended for direct comparison. What matters most?
answers: A common scale and matching definitions
questions.feedback: Shared units and scales make the comparison meaningful.
choices: A common scale and matching definitions
Different scale ranges chosen for visual balance
The same background colour on each chart

questions.question: A shop wants to know which of two product shares, 24% or 26%, is larger. Which display helps compare them?
answers: Bars using one shared scale
questions.feedback: Lengths along a shared baseline are easy to compare.
choices: Bars using one shared scale
Three-dimensional slices viewed from above
Two circles with unrelated sizes

cards: Why start bars at zero?
Their visible lengths should be proportional to the magnitudes.
How do you find a sector angle?
Multiply the category's fraction of the whole by 360 degrees.
When do overlapping categories rule out a pie?
When an observation can be counted in multiple shares of the same denominator.

questions.question: What appears on a histogram's horizontal axis?
answers: Intervals on a numeric measurement scale
questions.feedback: The measurement determines the rectangle positions.
choices: Intervals on a numeric measurement scale
Unordered names of the data categories
The relative frequency of each observation

questions.question: Where do equal-width count rectangles touch?
answers: At their shared numeric class boundaries
questions.feedback: Adjacent classes meet at their shared endpoint.
choices: At their shared numeric class boundaries
At the median value of the entire dataset
Only when they contain the same frequency

questions.question: A class has frequency zero. What do you draw?
answers: A zero-height rectangle over its span
questions.feedback: Zero counts still correspond to a real interval.
choices: A zero-height rectangle over its span
A gap that removes its interval from the scale
A rectangle the same height as its neighbour

questions.question: A class has width 4 and frequency 10. Give its frequency density.
questions.feedback: Divide 10 by 4.

questions.question: On a frequency-density histogram, what gives the count?
answers: Width multiplied by height
questions.feedback: The rectangle's area represents frequency.
choices: Width multiplied by height
Height divided by the full range
Width plus the height of the rectangle

questions.question: Two rectangles have equal areas but different widths. What is equal?
answers: Their class frequencies
questions.feedback: Equal area means equal count.
choices: Their class frequencies
Their vertical densities
Their class midpoints

questions.question: A width-10 class has count 5. Give its density.
questions.feedback: Five observations over ten units gives 0.5.

questions.question: What should two directly compared histograms share?
answers: Class boundaries and compatible scales
questions.feedback: Shared boundaries support direct comparisons.
choices: Class boundaries and compatible scales
Only the colour and the title font
A different unit for each dataset

questions.question: One class is twice as wide as another with the same count. What happens to density?
answers: It is half as high in the wider class
questions.feedback: The same area is spread over twice the width.
choices: It is half as high in the wider class
It is twice as high in the wider class
It stays equal to the narrower density

questions.question: A school report only has an open-ended highest class. What can you safely do?
answers: Keep that count in a table and explain the open boundary
questions.feedback: The width and density cannot be recovered from an open class.
choices: Keep that count in a table and explain the open boundary
Invent an upper endpoint from the previous class width
Draw a density bar whose width has no numeric meaning

questions.question: A gap appears with one bin scheme but vanishes with another. What should you report?
answers: The apparent gap depends on grouping
questions.feedback: The same observations can look different under another grouping.
choices: The apparent gap depends on grouping
The data changed when the bins changed
The second chart should be ignored automatically

cards: What does area mean on a frequency-density histogram?
Class frequency.
How do you compute frequency density?
Class frequency divided by class width.
What remains for a class with frequency zero?
Its horizontal span, with zero height.

questions.question: What is the running total after counts 3, 4 and 2?
answers: nine
questions.feedback: Add all three class counts.

questions.question: What does the final cumulative count equal?
answers: The number of valid included observations
questions.feedback: Every valid row has been counted once.
choices: The number of valid included observations
The number of interval labels displayed
The sum of the original measured values

questions.question: If the counts are 3, 4, 2 and 3, how many are below the second upper boundary?
answers: seven
questions.feedback: Add the first two counts.

questions.question: Where does each cumulative point go?
answers: At the upper boundary of its class
questions.feedback: The running count includes the whole class up to its upper edge.
choices: At the upper boundary of its class
At the midpoint of the class
At the smallest observed value in the class

questions.question: What does a level segment between grouped points indicate?
answers: Zero observations in that class
questions.feedback: The cumulative count did not increase.
choices: Zero observations in that class
A negative frequency in the class
The highest observed value in the class

questions.question: What is the final cumulative percentage with valid observations?
answers: 100 percent
questions.feedback: The entire included group has been counted.

questions.question: At a halfway point between totals 7 and 9, what does linear interpolation give?
answers: eight
questions.feedback: Half the rise of two adds one to seven.

questions.question: Is the interpolated 8 necessarily the true count?
answers: No, values may cluster within the interval
questions.feedback: The grouped table does not show positions inside a class.
choices: No, values may cluster within the interval
Yes, any cumulative chart gives all raw values
Yes, if the endpoint counts are both odd

questions.question: The cumulative counts below 5 and below 10 are 12 and 26. How many are at least 5 but below 10?
answers: fourteen
questions.feedback: Subtract 12 from 26.

questions.question: Your target lies halfway through a busy class. What gives the exact number that met it?
answers: The raw records or a boundary at the target
questions.feedback: Only a matching boundary or raw values resolves it.
choices: The raw records or a boundary at the target
The linearly interpolated count rounded down
The total count of the busiest class

questions.question: A cumulative chart drops from 20 to 18 at the next boundary. What should you check?
answers: An error in accumulation or plotting
questions.feedback: Running totals of nonnegative counts cannot decrease.
choices: An error in accumulation or plotting
A negative change in the dataset's sample size
Whether the next interval was especially wide

cards: What is an ogive?
A plot of cumulative count or percentage against a boundary.
How do you get a class count from adjacent cumulative counts?
Subtract the earlier total from the later total.
What does a straight segment between points assume for an estimate?
The count accumulates evenly across that interval.

questions.question: With key 2 vertical bar 7 = 27 minutes, what does stem 4 leaf 2 mean?

answers: Stem 4 and leaf 0

Stem 0 and leaf 4
Stem 4 with no leaf

questions.question: Why include a key?
answers: To show the scale and units of a pair
questions.feedback: A pair alone might stand for 27 or 2.7.

To show the total of all numeric values
To mark which data point was recorded first

questions.question: How many values does the row with leaves 1 5 5 7 represent?

questions.feedback: Both copies of leaf 5 count.

questions.question: What does a blank stem between occupied rows indicate?

questions.feedback: A blank row maintains the scale.
questions.part: Recover values and inspect the shape
choices: No observations in that span
One unknown value in that span
An omitted stem of unknown size

questions.question: Which has recoverable individual values at the stated precision?
answers: A stem-and-leaf plot with a key
questions.feedback: Reading leaves recovers the values.
questions.part: Recover values and inspect the shape
choices: A stem-and-leaf plot with a key
A histogram of broad grouped classes
A table showing only the total frequency

questions.question: A stem is crowded. What is a consistent split?
answers: First leaves 0–4, then leaves 5–9
questions.feedback: The two ranges partition the possible digits.
questions.part: Choose a scale that suits the data
choices: First leaves 0–4, then leaves 5–9
First duplicates, then single occurrences
First odd leaves, then all observed leaves

questions.question: Why use the same key for two groups?
answers: So a given stem and leaf mean the same value
questions.feedback: Comparisons require common units and scaling.
questions.part: Choose a scale that suits the data
choices: So a given stem and leaf mean the same value
So the groups must have the same sample size
So every row will have the same number of leaves

questions.question: A plot of rainfall uses key 1 vertical bar 2 = 1.2 cm. What is 3 vertical bar 4?
answers: 3.4 cm
questions.feedback: The leaf represents tenths of a centimetre.

questions.question: You read back 9 leaves from 10 valid records. What should you do?
answers: Retally and check that repeats were retained
questions.feedback: The plot must preserve every valid record.
questions.part: Recover values and inspect the shape
choices: Retally and check that repeats were retained
Delete the record that does not fit the plot
Add a blank leaf beside the smallest stem

questions.question: A plot was built after rounding to whole minutes. Can it recover 12.3 minutes exactly?
answers: No, it can recover only the displayed precision
questions.feedback: Rounding loses the fractional information.
questions.part: Choose a scale that suits the data
choices: No, it can recover only the displayed precision
Yes, count the repeated leaves in the row
Yes, as long as a key was included

cards: What does the key tell you?
The numeric value and unit represented by a stem and leaf.
How do you show duplicates?
Write the same leaf once for each occurrence.
What does an empty stem mean?
No included observations in that span.

questions.question: Bars for 98 and 100 start at 97. What is misleading?
answers: The visible length ratio differs from the count ratio
questions.feedback: Lengths 1 and 3 misrepresent amounts 98 and 100.
choices: The visible length ratio differs from the count ratio
The total should have been divided by two first
The bars should have used narrower categories

questions.question: If a square icon doubles in width and height, what happens to its area?
answers: four
4 times
four times
questions.feedback: Two times two gives four times the area.

questions.question: What represents frequency in a density histogram?
answers: Rectangle area over a class interval
questions.feedback: Area is height times width.
choices: Rectangle area over a class interval
Horizontal position of its highest point
The number printed below each interval

cards: How do you find a median?
Put the data in order and take the middle value, or the mean of the middle two.
When is the median better than the mean?
When the data are skewed or have outliers.
What's the sample variance formula?
The sum of (value - mean) squared, divided by n - 1.
How's standard deviation related to variance?
It's the square root of the variance, so it's in the original units.
What's a z-score?
(value - mean) / SD. It's how many standard deviations a value is from the mean.
What does the empirical rule say?
In bell-shaped data, about 68%, 95% and 99.7% lie within 1, 2 and 3 SDs of the mean.

Q3 minus Q1.
